translations.title: Almacén Propio, Operador Logístico O FBA: Cuál Conviene Para Vender En México
translations.excerpt: La decisión no es cuál es mejor sino cuál corresponde a su volumen actual y al que espera en seis meses. Las tres opciones son correctas en algún punto de esa curva y equivocadas fuera de él.

translations.metaTitle: Almacén Propio, Operador Logístico O FBA En México
translations.metaDescription: Tres formas de guardar y despachar inventario en México, con lo que cada una cuesta de verdad, lo que exige de usted y el momento en que deja de convenir.
keywords: almacén propio vs operador logístico México
translations.content:
Con volumen bajo o irregular conviene un operador logístico, porque convierte costos fijos en variables. Con volumen alto y estable puede convenir un almacén propio. FBA conviene cuando la velocidad dentro del marketplace vale más que el control. La pregunta no es cuál es mejor, sino en qué punto de esa curva está usted hoy.

  • Las tres opciones no compiten en el mismo tramo de volumen; cada una gana en un rango distinto.
  • El costo por unidad de un operador logístico baja con el volumen, pero el de un almacén propio baja más rápido una vez superado el punto de equilibrio.
  • FBA optimiza para la entrega rápida dentro del marketplace, no para el costo de almacenar durante meses.
  • Cambiar de modelo tiene un costo de transición que casi nunca se incluye en la comparación y que suele decidirla.

¿Qué compara realmente cada opción?

No compara precios. Compara qué parte de la operación asume usted y qué parte delega.

Las tres opciones suelen presentarse como tres precios, y esa es la razón por la que la comparación casi siempre sale mal. Almacén propio. Usted renta el espacio, contrata al personal, compra o alquila el equipo, define los procesos y responde por los errores. El costo es en su mayoría fijo: se paga completo tanto en un mes de temporada alta como en uno muerto. Operador logístico. Un tercero guarda su inventario y despacha sus pedidos en su nombre. El costo es en su mayoría variable: se paga por espacio ocupado y por pedido procesado. Usted delega la ejecución y conserva la decisión. FBA. El marketplace guarda y despacha, y a cambio su producto entra en la promesa de entrega del marketplace. Usted delega ejecución y también parte de la decisión, porque el marketplace fija sus propias reglas de recepción, de almacenamiento y de retiro. Visto así, la comparación deja de ser de precios y pasa a ser de estructura de costos y de control. Y eso sí se puede decidir con números.

¿En qué tramo de volumen gana cada opción?

Volumen bajo e irregular: operador logístico. Alto y estable: almacén propio. Velocidad dentro del marketplace: FBA.

Volumen bajo o irregular. Aquí el operador logístico gana casi siempre, y no por poco. Un almacén propio con la mitad del espacio vacío sigue costando lo mismo, mientras que con un tercero usted paga por lo que ocupa. Además evita el desembolso inicial, el contrato de arrendamiento y la contratación, que son compromisos difíciles de revertir si la demanda no aparece. Volumen alto y estable. Aquí la aritmética se invierte. El costo por unidad de un operador logístico baja con el volumen pero no desaparece, porque incluye su margen. Llegado cierto punto, ese margen acumulado supera lo que costaría operar usted mismo. La palabra que decide es *estable*: un almacén propio castiga la estacionalidad, porque el costo fijo no baja en los meses flojos. Velocidad dentro del marketplace. FBA gana cuando la visibilidad y la promesa de entrega del marketplace mueven más ventas de las que cuesta el servicio. Deja de ganar cuando el inventario rota lento, porque entonces aparecen los cargos por almacenamiento prolongado, o cuando usted vende también fuera del marketplace y necesita el mismo inventario disponible en otros canales.

¿Qué costos no aparecen en ninguna cotización?

Espacio vacío, tiempo de gestión, errores y transición.

Cuatro renglones deciden más comparaciones que la tarifa, y ninguno de los cuatro figura en una cotización. El espacio vacío. En un almacén propio se paga completo. Si su ocupación promedio es del sesenta por ciento, su costo real por unidad es bastante mayor al que calculó dividiendo la renta entre la capacidad. Su tiempo. Operar un almacén consume atención directiva: personal, incidencias, inventarios, proveedores. Ese tiempo tiene un costo de oportunidad, y en una operación pequeña suele ser el recurso más escaso que existe. Los errores. Un pedido mal surtido cuesta la devolución, el reemplazo y, en un marketplace, el golpe a la métrica. Al comparar, pregunte por la exactitud medida por pedido y no por línea, porque es la cifra que corresponde a lo que verá su cliente. La transición. Cambiar de modelo implica mover inventario, reconfigurar integraciones y operar en paralelo un tiempo. Es un costo real, se paga una sola vez y decide más comparaciones ajustadas de lo que la gente supone. Inclúyalo antes de decidir, no después.

¿Cómo hacer la cuenta con sus propios números?

Costo total mensual dividido entre pedidos despachados, proyectado a doce meses y no a uno.

La comparación honesta cabe en cuatro pasos y no requiere un modelo complicado. Uno. Sume el costo mensual total de cada opción, con todos los renglones. Para el almacén propio: renta, personal, equipo, servicios, seguros, sistemas. Para el operador logístico: almacenamiento, recepción, procesamiento por pedido, materiales, cargos por manejo especial. Para FBA: tarifas de logística, almacenamiento mensual y cualquier cargo por permanencia prolongada según su rotación. Dos. Divida entre los pedidos que despacha al mes. Ese es su costo por pedido real, y suele diferir bastante del que aparece en la tarifa. Tres. Repita el cálculo con el volumen que espera en doce meses. Una opción que gana hoy puede perder cuando duplique el volumen, y mudarse cuesta. Cuatro. Haga el mismo cálculo con el sesenta por ciento del volumen esperado. Si una opción se vuelve insostenible en ese escenario, está comprando un riesgo además de un servicio, y conviene saberlo antes de firmar.

¿Cuándo llegó el momento de cambiar de modelo?

Cuando el costo por pedido deja de bajar, cuando el espacio sobra o cuando la operación consume la atención del negocio.

Ninguna decisión de estas es permanente. Estas son las señales que indican que el modelo actual dejó de corresponder. Su costo por pedido se estancó pese a que el volumen creció. Con un operador logístico esto indica que su margen ya pesa más que la eficiencia que aporta, y conviene renegociar o evaluar espacio propio. Paga por espacio que no usa de forma sostenida. En almacén propio es la señal más clara de que el modelo quedó grande. En FBA, con rotación lenta, aparece primero como cargos por almacenamiento prolongado. La operación consume su atención. Si las incidencias de almacén ocupan la agenda que debería estar en producto y en ventas, el modelo está cobrando un precio que no aparece en ninguna factura. Necesita el mismo inventario en varios canales. Es la señal típica de que la dependencia exclusiva de un marketplace empezó a limitar el crecimiento, y suele resolverse con inventario disponible en un punto que sirva a todos los canales.

Dónde entramos nosotros en esta comparación

BringGo Ship opera como el segundo de los tres modelos, con bodegas propias en Laredo, Texas y en Monterrey, y le decimos con franqueza cuándo no somos la respuesta. Si su volumen es alto, estable y de un solo canal, hay un punto en el que un almacén propio le sale más barato que nosotros, y preferimos que haga esa cuenta antes de contratar y no dieciocho meses después. Lo que sí podemos hacer es darle las cifras que necesita para hacerla: costo por pedido real, ocupación promedio y exactitud medida por pedido. Con esas tres, la comparación se decide sola.

Definiciones

  • Costo fijo: El que se paga completo con independencia del volumen despachado, como la renta de una bodega.
  • Costo variable: El que sube y baja con el volumen, como el cargo por pedido procesado de un operador logístico.
  • Punto de equilibrio: El volumen a partir del cual una opción con costo fijo alto resulta más barata por unidad que una con costo variable.
  • Costo de transición: Lo que cuesta una sola vez cambiar de modelo: mover inventario, reconfigurar integraciones y operar en paralelo.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Qué conviene si apenas estoy empezando a vender en México?

Casi siempre un operador logístico. Convierte costos fijos en variables, evita el arrendamiento y la contratación, y le permite equivocarse en el pronóstico de demanda sin pagar por espacio vacío durante meses.

¿En qué momento conviene una bodega propia?

Cuando el volumen es alto y, sobre todo, estable. La palabra que decide es estable: el costo fijo no baja en los meses flojos, así que una operación estacional puede tener el volumen suficiente y aun así perder con este modelo.

¿Puedo combinar FBA con un almacén en México?

Sí, y es común. Se guarda el inventario en un punto propio o de un operador y se envía al marketplace por reposiciones, lo que reduce la exposición a cargos por almacenamiento prolongado y deja inventario disponible para otros canales.

¿Cómo comparo cotizaciones que están estructuradas distinto?

Llévelas todas a una sola cifra: costo total mensual dividido entre pedidos despachados. Es la única forma de comparar una tarifa por metro cuadrado con una por pedido, y suele cambiar el orden de las opciones.

¿Qué costo se olvida con más frecuencia?

El de transición. Mover inventario, reconfigurar integraciones y operar en paralelo un tiempo se paga una sola vez, pero decide muchas comparaciones ajustadas. Inclúyalo antes de firmar y no después de haberse mudado.

translations.excerpt: FBM, satıcının ürünü kendi depoladığı ve kargoladığı modeldir. Amazon Meksika'da nasıl çalışır, FBA'den nasıl ayrılır ve Prime için neden ayrı bir yol gerekir? İşte tamamı.

translations.metaTitle: Amazon Meksika FBM Nedir, FBA'den Farkı ve Prime Rozeti
translations.metaDescription: Amazon Meksika'da FBM nedir, nasıl çalışır? Satıcının kendi kargoladığı model, FBA ile farkı ve Meksika'da Prime rozetinin neden NARF gerektirdiği.
keywords: amazon meksika fbm nedir nasıl yapılır
translations.content:
Amazon Meksika'da FBM (Fulfillment by Merchant), satıcının ürünü kendi deposunda tuttuğu, siparişi kendi paketleyip kargoladığı ve müşteri hizmeti ile iadeleri kendi yönettiği modeldir. FNSKU ve Amazon hazırlık kuralları gerektirmez, ama otomatik Prime rozeti de vermez. Meksika'da ABD stoğundan Prime satmanın yolu FBM değil, NARF (uzaktan FBA) programıdır.

  • FBM (Fulfillment by Merchant), satıcının ürünü kendi depolayıp paketleyip kargoladığı ve müşteri hizmeti ile iadeleri kendi yönettiği modeldir (Amazon).
  • FBM, FNSKU etiketi ve Amazon hazırlık kurallarını gerektirmez, ama otomatik Prime rozeti de vermez.
  • Satıcının kendi kargolayarak Prime kazanmasını sağlayan Seller Fulfilled Prime (SFP) yalnızca ABD pazarında geçerlidir; Meksika (amazon.com.mx) SFP pazarı değildir (Amazon).
  • Meksika'da ABD stoğundan Prime satmak için yol NARF, yani uzaktan FBA programıdır (FNSKU kullanır), FBM değil.
  • FBM'de iade taleplerine 24 saat içinde yanıt vermek ve hesap sağlığı eşiklerini korumak gerekir (Amazon).

Amazon Meksika'da FBM nasıl çalışır?

Satıcı ürünü kendi deposunda tutar, sipariş gelince kendisi paketleyip kargolar, müşteri hizmeti ve iadeleri kendisi yönetir. Amazon depolamaz veya kargolamaz. FNSKU ve Amazon hazırlık kuralları gerekmez; buna karşılık otomatik Prime rozeti de yoktur. Kontrol sizde, sorumluluk da sizdedir.

Amazon Meksika'da FBM, yani Fulfillment by Merchant, en yalın modeldir: ürünü Amazon değil, satıcı yönetir. İşleyiş şöyle: ürünü kendi deponuzda veya bir üçüncü parti depoda tutarsınız; amazon.com.mx'te bir sipariş geldiğinde ürünü kendiniz paketler ve kendi kargo anlaşmanızla veya Amazon'un Satın Al Kargo aracıyla gönderirsiniz; müşteri hizmetini ve iadeleri de kendiniz yürütürsünüz. Amazon bu modelde depolama, paketleme veya kargo yapmaz; sadece pazar yerini ve tahsilatı sağlar. Bunun iki yüzü vardır. Avantaj tarafında, FBM tam kontrol demektir: stok Amazon'un deposunda kilitli değildir, FNSKU etiketi ve Amazon'un hazırlık kuralları gerekmez, ve birim başına fulfillment maliyeti genellikle daha düşüktür. Dezavantaj tarafında, tüm operasyon sizin sorumluluğunuzdadır ve en önemlisi, FBM otomatik Prime rozeti getirmez; oysa Meksikalı alıcı hızlı teslimatı ve Prime'ı önemser. Yani FBM, kontrolü ve düşük maliyeti önceleyen, kendi lojistiğini yönetebilen satıcı için mantıklıdır. Pratikte birçok satıcı FBM ve FBA'yi ürün bazında birlikte kullanır: bazı ürünleri kendi kargolar, bazılarını Amazon'a bırakır. BringGo Ship, Meksika içindeki deposuyla FBM için gereken yerel depolama ve kargo altyapısını sağlar, böylece kendi kargonuzu yönetseniz de Meksika içinden hızlı gönderirsiniz.

FBM ile FBA arasındaki fark nedir?

FBA'de Amazon depolar, paketler, kargolar ve iadeleri yönetir; otomatik Prime verir ama FNSKU ve hazırlık kuralları ister. FBM'de bunları satıcı yapar; FNSKU ve hazırlık gerekmez, birim maliyet düşük olabilir ama otomatik Prime yoktur. İkisi ürün bazında aynı hesapta birlikte kullanılabilir.

FBM ile FBA arasındaki farkı netleştirmek, hangi ürün için hangisini seçeceğinizi belirler. FBA, yani Fulfillment by Amazon, ürününüzü Amazon'un depolarına gönderdiğiniz modeldir: Amazon depolar, sipariş gelince paketler ve kargolar, müşteri hizmeti ve iadelerin çoğunu yönetir. Karşılığında iki şey ister: ürünlerin FNSKU ile etiketlenmesi ve Amazon'un hazırlık kurallarına uyulması. Buna karşılık otomatik Prime rozeti verir, ki bu dönüşümü ciddi biçimde artırır. FBM ise bunun tersidir: depolama, paketleme, kargo, müşteri hizmeti ve iadeler satıcıdadır; FNSKU ve hazırlık kuralları gerekmez; birim başına fulfillment maliyeti genellikle daha düşüktür ve stok üzerinde tam kontrol sizdedir; ama otomatik Prime yoktur. Karar verirken üç soruyu sorun: kendi lojistiğimi hızlı ve güvenilir yönetebilir miyim, bu ürün için Prime rozeti ne kadar kritik, ve birim maliyet ile kontrol mü yoksa Prime ve kolaylık mı benim için önemli. Çoğu deneyimli satıcı ikisini birlikte kullanır: yüksek hacimli, Prime'ın kritik olduğu ürünleri FBA'ye koyar; büyük, ağır veya yavaş dönen ya da kendi kargolamayı tercih ettiği ürünleri FBM'de tutar. Bu ikisi aynı hesapta ürün bazında rahatça birlikte çalışır. BringGo Ship, FBM için yerel depolama ve kargo, FBA için ise ürünü Meksika'ya ithal edip hazırlama tarafında destek verir; böylece iki modeli de tek operasyondan besleyebilirsiniz.

FBM ile Meksika'da Prime satabilir miyim?

Hayır, FBM Meksika'da otomatik Prime vermez ve satıcının kendi kargolayarak Prime kazanmasını sağlayan Seller Fulfilled Prime yalnızca ABD pazarında geçerlidir; Meksika SFP pazarı değildir. ABD stoğundan Meksika'da Prime satmanın yolu NARF, yani uzaktan FBA programıdır, FBM değil.

Bu, en çok karıştırılan ve yanlış yönlendirmenin en kolay olduğu noktadır, o yüzden net olalım. FBM, Meksika'da otomatik Prime rozeti getirmez. Peki satıcı kendi kargolayarak Prime kazanamaz mı? ABD'de bunun bir yolu vardır: Seller Fulfilled Prime, yani SFP, satıcının kendi deposundan kargolayıp yine de Prime rozeti taşımasını sağlar. Ancak kritik nokta şudur: SFP yalnızca ABD pazarında geçerlidir ve ABD içi bir varsayılan kargo adresi gerektirir; Meksika, yani amazon.com.mx, bir SFP pazarı değildir. Dolayısıyla Meksika'da bir FBM ilanının Prime rozeti alacağını söylemek yanlıştır; bu, ABD'ye özel SFP ile Meksika'yı karıştırmaktır. Peki Meksika'da ABD stoğundan Prime nasıl satılır? Yolu FBM değil, NARF'tır, yani Remote Fulfillment with FBA, uzaktan FBA programı. NARF, ABD'deki FBA stoğunuzu Meksika'da Prime ile satmanızı sağlar; Amazon sınır ötesi taşıma, gümrük ve teslimatı üstlenir ve bu bir FBA programı olduğu için FNSKU kullanır. Özetle: Meksika'da hızlı, yerel Prime istiyorsanız iki gerçek yol vardır: ya ürünü Meksika'ya ithal edip yerel FBA yapmak, ya da ABD stoğundan NARF ile satmak. FBM, kontrol ve düşük maliyet için iyidir ama Prime için değil. BringGo Ship, yerel FBA'ye geçmek istediğinizde ithalat, gümrük ve Meksika içi stoklamayı üstlenir.

Tanımlar

  • FBM: FBM (Fulfillment by Merchant), satıcının ürünü kendi depolayıp paketleyip kargoladığı ve müşteri hizmeti ile iadeleri kendi yönettiği modeldir.
  • Seller Fulfilled Prime (SFP): SFP, satıcının kendi deposundan kargolayarak Prime rozeti kazandığı programdır ve yalnızca ABD pazarında geçerlidir.
  • NARF: NARF (uzaktan FBA), ABD FBA stoğundan Meksika'da Prime ile satmayı sağlayan programdır ve FNSKU kullanır.

Sık sorulan sorular

Amazon Meksika'da FBM nedir?

FBM (Fulfillment by Merchant), satıcının ürünü kendi deposunda tuttuğu, sipariş gelince kendisi paketleyip kargoladığı ve müşteri hizmeti ile iadeleri kendi yönettiği modeldir. Amazon depolamaz veya kargolamaz. FNSKU ve hazırlık kuralları gerekmez; buna karşılık otomatik Prime rozeti de vermez.

FBM ile FBA arasındaki fark nedir?

FBA'de Amazon depolar, paketler, kargolar ve iadeleri yönetir; otomatik Prime verir ama FNSKU ve hazırlık kuralları ister. FBM'de bunları satıcı yapar; FNSKU ve hazırlık gerekmez, birim maliyet düşük olabilir ama otomatik Prime yoktur. İkisi ürün bazında aynı hesapta birlikte kullanılabilir.

FBM ile Meksika'da Prime satabilir miyim?

Hayır. FBM Meksika'da otomatik Prime vermez ve satıcının kendi kargolayarak Prime kazanmasını sağlayan Seller Fulfilled Prime yalnızca ABD pazarında geçerlidir; Meksika SFP pazarı değildir. ABD stoğundan Meksika'da Prime satmanın yolu NARF, yani uzaktan FBA programıdır.

Meksika'da Prime rozeti nasıl alınır?

İki gerçek yol vardır: ürünü Meksika'ya ithal edip yerel FBA yapmak, ya da ABD stoğundan NARF (uzaktan FBA) ile satmak. Her ikisi de FBA programı olduğu için Prime rozeti getirir. FBM bu rozeti getirmez, çünkü SFP ABD'ye özeldir ve Meksika'yı kapsamaz.

FBM'de satıcının sorumlulukları nelerdir?

Stok bilgisini güncel tutmak, gönderiyi işlem süresinde geçerli takip numarasıyla onaylamak, iade taleplerine 24 saat içinde yanıt vermek ve hesap sağlığı eşiklerini (geç gönderim, sipariş kusur oranı gibi) korumak. Bunlar aksarsa hesabın performansı zarar görür.

FBM ve FBA'yi birlikte kullanabilir miyim?

Evet. İkisi aynı hesapta ürün bazında birlikte çalışır. Çoğu deneyimli satıcı, Prime'ın kritik olduğu yüksek hacimli ürünleri FBA'ye koyar; büyük, ağır veya yavaş dönen ürünleri ise FBM'de kendi kargolar. Bu esneklik, her ürün için en uygun modeli seçmenizi sağlar.

Amazon Mexico FBA prep requires each unit to carry the correct barcode, an FNSKU sticker where a scannable manufacturer barcode is not used, on a compliant label, with packaging that protects the item and meets Amazon's rules. On top of Amazon's prep, goods imported into Mexico also need Spanish NOM labeling to clear customs, which is a separate requirement. What are Amazon Mexico's FBA prep and labeling requirements?

Each unit needs a scannable barcode, an FNSKU sticker where a manufacturer barcode is not used, on a compliant black-on-white removable label that covers any original barcode, plus packaging that protects the item and meets Amazon's rules. Separately, goods imported into Mexico need Spanish NOM labeling to clear customs.

Amazon Mexico FBA prep follows the same global FBA logic, and getting it right is what keeps your inventory from being rejected or held. The core requirement is the barcode: every unit must carry a scannable barcode so Amazon can identify it. When a product has a scannable manufacturer barcode and you use stickerless commingled inventory, that can serve, but in many cases you need an FNSKU, Amazon's own barcode that ties one unit to one seller. The FNSKU is generated in Seller Central and printed on a compliant label: black ink on a white, non-reflective removable label, roughly 1x2 to 2x3 inches, placed on a flat surface and covering any original barcode so that only one barcode scans, and showing the scannable code, the FNSKU, the product title and its condition. Beyond the barcode, packaging matters: units must be packaged to protect them and to meet Amazon's prep rules, which for certain products means poly-bagging with a suffocation warning, bubble wrapping fragile items, or bundling sets securely so they stay together. What is easy to miss is that FBA prep is not the only labeling your goods need. To be imported into Mexico at all, most retail goods must carry Spanish NOM labeling, and that is a separate legal requirement from Amazon's prep, one for customs and one for the fulfillment center. So Amazon Mexico inventory is meeting two rulebooks at once: Amazon's prep for the FC, and Mexico's NOM labeling for customs. How do the 2026 prep changes affect Mexico?

Carefully, because they were announced for the US. Amazon ended some US FBA prep services and commingling in 2026, meaning US sellers must prep themselves. Those announcements came through US Seller Central and refer to US FBA, so do not assume they apply to Amazon Mexico fulfillment centers; verify Mexico applicability before relying on them.

Two 2026 changes to Amazon's prep are worth flagging, along with the important caveat about where they apply. First, effective at the start of 2026, Amazon ended some of its US FBA prep and item-labeling services, the ones where Amazon would apply FNSKU stickers, poly-bag, bubble-wrap or bundle items for you, so US sellers must now prep and label their inventory themselves before it arrives, and shipments created without proper prep are not eligible for damage or loss reimbursement. Second, for inventory shipped from a certain 2026 date, Amazon ended commingling with new rules that require many resellers to apply FNSKU stickers to all FBA inventory even when a manufacturer barcode is present. Here is the crucial point: both of these were announced through US Seller Central and refer to US FBA policy. It would be a mistake to assume they apply identically to Amazon Mexico fulfillment centers, because Mexico applicability was not separately confirmed in the same announcements. The safe way to treat them is as US FBA policy that you should verify for Mexico rather than apply blindly. What is genuinely global is the core FNSKU mechanics, the barcode, the label specs, the packaging, which apply to Mexico too. So the practical rule is to always prep and label your inventory yourself, treat the specific 2026 dated changes as US policy to confirm for Mexico, and keep the Spanish NOM labeling as a separate customs requirement regardless. Generate FNSKU labels in Seller Central, apply them correctly on compliant labels covering any original barcode, package units to Amazon's rules, and apply Spanish NOM labeling for customs, all before the goods cross. Doing the prep and the NOM labeling at a border warehouse means inventory arrives ready for both customs and Amazon.

Fifth, do all of this at a border warehouse before the goods cross, so the inventory clears Mexican customs correctly labeled and arrives at the Mexican fulfillment center already prepped, rather than discovering a prep or labeling problem after the crossing when it is expensive to fix. The efficiency comes from doing the FBA prep and the NOM labeling in the same place, at the same time, on the same inventory. That is exactly what a border prep operation is for. translations.title: Amazon Mexico Tax Withholding For Foreign Sellers: IVA And ISR Explained
translations.excerpt: Selling on Amazon Mexico without a Mexican tax registration is not just a compliance gap. It is a direct and immediate hit to your cash flow, applied to every order.
translations.coverAlt: Person reviewing financial statements and tax documents at a desk, photographic, no text
translations.metaTitle: Amazon Mexico Tax Withholding: IVA and ISR Without an RFC
translations.metaDescription: Without a Mexican RFC, Amazon withholds 20 percent ISR and the full 16 percent IVA from your sales. How the withholding works and how to reduce it.
translations.content:
Amazon Mexico withholds tax from marketplace sellers at source. A seller who has not provided a valid Mexican RFC faces the maximum rates: 20 percent ISR on the sale price and the full 16 percent IVA. Sellers with a registered RFC face substantially lower ISR withholding, and registered taxpayers can credit withheld IVA against their own liability. The withholding is applied by Amazon and remitted to SAT; it is not optional and it is not negotiable.

  • Without a valid RFC, ISR withholding is 20 percent of the sale price, applied regardless of your actual margin.
  • Without an RFC, or where funds are paid to a foreign bank account, platforms withhold 100 percent of the IVA, which at the standard rate means 16 percent.
  • Mexico's 2026 tax framework extended automatic withholding across digital platforms including Amazon and Mercado Libre, for both individuals and companies.
  • IVA withheld from a registered taxpayer can be credited; IVA withheld from an unregistered foreign seller generally cannot be recovered.
  • Withholding is calculated on the sale price, not on profit, which is why it hits low-margin categories hardest.

What does Amazon withhold and at what rate?

Two separate taxes. ISR at 20 percent of the sale price for sellers without an RFC, and IVA at the full 16 percent where no RFC is provided or funds go to a foreign account.

Mexico requires digital platforms to withhold tax at source from the sellers who trade on them. Amazon does not choose to do this; it is a legal obligation, and the amount depends on what you have told Amazon about your tax status. ISR is income tax. For a seller without a valid RFC the withholding is 20 percent of the sale price. Read that carefully: the sale price, not the profit. A seller running a 15 percent margin does not pay 20 percent of the margin, they lose more than the margin itself on that transaction. IVA is value added tax, standard rate 16 percent. Where the seller has not provided an RFC, or where proceeds are paid to a foreign bank account, the platform withholds the entire IVA rather than a partial share. The two stack. A seller without an RFC selling into Mexico sees both applied to the same transaction, and the combined effect is severe enough that many sellers discover their Mexico operation was never profitable once the first settlement report arrives.

Why does the RFC change the outcome so much?

The maximum rates function as a default for unidentified taxpayers. Registration moves you into the ordinary regime with lower rates and recoverable IVA.

The high withholding is not a penalty in the formal sense, but it works like one. Mexico's tax authority cannot assess a seller it cannot identify, so the system withholds at the top of the range and leaves it to the seller to register and reconcile. Once you have a valid RFC and the platform has it on file, two things change. ISR withholding falls to the rate applicable to your regime rather than the punitive default. And withheld IVA becomes creditable: as a registered taxpayer you offset it against the IVA you charge and owe, so it stops being a permanent cost and becomes a timing difference. For a foreign seller without Mexican registration, withheld IVA is generally not recoverable. That is the part sellers underestimate. The ISR is painful but visible; the unrecoverable IVA is a silent 16 percent that never comes back. This is why the RFC question is not a paperwork preference. It determines whether roughly a third of your revenue is a tax cost or a recoverable balance.

What are the options for a foreign seller?

Register a Mexican entity and obtain an RFC, work through a structure that holds the RFC, or accept the maximum withholding as a cost of doing business.

Establishing a Mexican entity gives you an RFC, access to the ordinary tax regime, creditable IVA and the ability to enrol in the padrón de importadores so you can import in your own name. The cost is time, professional fees and ongoing filing obligations, including monthly returns whether or not you traded. Operating through a structure that holds the Mexican tax registration is what many cross-border sellers use, particularly when combined with an importer of record arrangement. It resolves the import side and the tax registration together. It is a real commercial relationship, so understand who bears which liability before signing. Accepting the withholding is a legitimate short-term choice while you test the market, provided you price for it. What does not work is pricing as though the withholding is not there and hoping to fix it later. The withholding applies from your first order. Whichever route you choose, model it before you launch. Take a representative SKU, apply 20 percent ISR and 16 percent IVA to the sale price, subtract landed cost and Amazon's referral and fulfillment fees, and see what remains. That number, not the gross margin, is your Mexico business case.

Proceeds to foreign bank accountApplies per regimeFull IVA withheld
Valid RFC, registered regimeRate per applicable regimeWithheld IVA creditable against liability

Definitions

  • RFC: The RFC (Registro Federal de Contribuyentes) is the Mexican tax identification number required for tax registration, importing and reduced platform withholding.
  • ISR: ISR (Impuesto Sobre la Renta) is Mexican income tax, withheld by marketplaces from seller proceeds at a rate that depends on the seller's registration status.
  • IVA: IVA (Impuesto al Valor Agregado) is Mexican value added tax at a standard rate of 16 percent, creditable by registered taxpayers and a sunk cost for unregistered foreign sellers.

Frequently asked questions

How much does Amazon Mexico withhold if I have no RFC?

20 percent ISR on the sale price plus the full 16 percent IVA. Both are calculated on the sale price rather than on profit, which is why the combined effect often exceeds a seller's gross margin.

Can I get the withheld IVA back?

A registered Mexican taxpayer can credit withheld IVA against IVA owed. A foreign seller without Mexican tax registration generally cannot recover it, so it becomes a permanent cost.

Do I need a Mexican company to get an RFC?

In practice, tax registration in Mexico requires either a Mexican legal entity or an individual with Mexican tax residency. Foreign sellers commonly work through a structure that holds the registration instead.

Is the withholding calculated on profit or on the sale price?

On the sale price. This is the detail that surprises most sellers, because a 20 percent withholding on revenue can exceed the entire margin on a low-margin product.

Does providing a bank account in Mexico change the withholding?

Paying proceeds to a foreign bank account triggers full IVA withholding. A Mexican account alone does not substitute for an RFC, but the combination of RFC and local account produces the ordinary treatment.

translations.excerpt: Yes, dropshipping to Mexico is legal. The real question is whether the taxes and customs rules leave you a margin. This 2026 explainer covers what applies and how to stay compliant.

translations.metaTitle: Is Dropshipping to Mexico Legal? 2026 Taxes and Duty Rules
translations.metaDescription: Dropshipping to Mexico is legal, but taxes and de minimis rules decide if it is profitable. What applies in 2026 and how to stay compliant.
translations.content:
Yes, dropshipping to Mexico is legal. There is no law against selling goods you do not hold in stock. What you must respect is import compliance: correct customs declarations, the 16 percent IVA, any duty, and the fact that Mexico's de minimis is only about 117 dollars for US-origin goods, so most parcels owe tax. Legality is easy; profitability depends on getting the tax and customs math right.

  • Dropshipping is a fulfillment model, not a regulated activity, so it is legal in Mexico when imports are declared correctly (SAT).
  • Mexico's de minimis is about 117 dollars duty-free for US-origin goods, with a flat 17 percent rate applying between 50 and 117 dollars (SAT courier regime).
  • US-origin goods generally clear at preferential USMCA rates; non-treaty origin faces the 2026 tariff decree (EY Mexico).
  • The US suspended duty-free de minimis on incoming goods from 29 August 2025, which affects reverse and return flows (CBP).
  • A local Mexican warehouse converts slow per-parcel imports into fast domestic dropshipping.

Is dropshipping from the US to Mexico legal?

Yes. Dropshipping is simply selling goods you do not physically stock, and no Mexican law prohibits it. The obligations are the ordinary ones of importing: declare goods correctly, pay IVA and any duty, and use a licensed broker for formal entries.

Dropshipping is a fulfillment method, not a special legal category. You list a product, the customer buys, and the item ships from a supplier or warehouse rather than from your own shelves. Nothing about that arrangement is illegal in Mexico. What people really mean when they ask if it is legal is whether they can do it without running into customs and tax problems, and the answer there is that you must follow the same import rules as any seller. Goods entering Mexico must be declared, most retail goods need Spanish NOM labeling, and taxes apply. The compliant way to dropship into Mexico is to make sure each shipment has a correct commercial invoice, the right product classification, and clears through proper channels, with a licensed agente aduanal for formal entries. BringGo Ship supports exactly this model, holding goods in its Laredo and Monterrey warehouses so orders ship domestically inside Mexico. Legality is not the hard part. The hard part is designing the flow so the taxes and customs do not eat your margin, which is a planning problem, not a legal one.

What taxes and customs costs apply to dropshipped orders?

Every import owes IVA of 16 percent above the small de minimis, plus any duty. Mexico's de minimis is only about 117 dollars for US-origin goods, so unlike some markets, most individual parcels are taxable.

This is where dropshipping to Mexico differs from markets with generous de minimis thresholds. Mexico allows roughly 50 dollars fully tax-free and up to about 117 dollars duty-free for US-origin goods under USMCA, but a flat 17 percent rate applies between 50 and 117 dollars, and 19 percent above 117 dollars, under Mexico's courier de minimis regime (SAT)'s reading of the rules. In practice that means most parcels of real retail value owe tax. Duty is a separate question decided by origin: US-origin goods with a valid certificate of origin generally clear at preferential USMCA rates, while goods that cannot prove qualifying origin, including many China-sourced items, face the 2026 tariff decree. So a dropshipper importing cheap non-US-origin goods parcel by parcel can be hit with both duty and IVA on every order, which destroys thin margins. The math only works if you either sell higher-value goods where the tax is a small percentage, or you change the model so goods enter Mexico in bulk once and ship domestically, spreading the import cost across many orders.

How do you dropship to Mexico profitably and compliantly?

Import in bulk to a Mexican warehouse, then fulfill domestically. This turns per-parcel customs into a one-time bulk clearance, cuts delivery times, and keeps every order compliant without repeating import costs on each sale.

The model that survives the tax math is to stop importing one parcel at a time. When you send inventory in bulk to a warehouse inside Mexico, you clear customs once, pay duty and IVA once on the batch, and then every customer order ships as a domestic parcel with no new border crossing. That spreads the import cost across many sales instead of stacking it on each one, and it collapses delivery from the week or more a cross-border parcel takes to the one to three days a domestic carrier needs. It also keeps you cleanly compliant, because a single well documented bulk import with correct labeling and a proper pedimento is far easier to get right than hundreds of individual parcel declarations. This hybrid approach, importing in bulk and dropshipping domestically, is what a border and in-country warehouse operator enables. BringGo Ship holds your stock in Laredo and Monterrey, prepares the entry file for the licensed broker who clears it, and ships orders inside Mexico, so the customer gets a fast domestic delivery and you get one clean import instead of a customs event on every order. That is how dropshipping to Mexico goes from legal-but-unprofitable to a working business.

The 16% rate is set in the value added tax law, and importing goods is one of the listed taxable activities:

Definitions

  • Dropshipping: Dropshipping is a retail model where the seller lists products they do not physically stock and fulfills each order from a supplier or warehouse.
  • De minimis: De minimis is the shipment value below which a country waives duty or tax, about 117 dollars duty-free for US-origin goods entering Mexico.
  • IVA: IVA is Mexico's value-added tax, 16 percent nationally, charged on the customs value of imports.

Frequently asked questions

Is dropshipping to Mexico legal in 2026?

Yes. Dropshipping is a fulfillment model, not a regulated activity, and no Mexican law prohibits it. You must follow ordinary import rules: declare goods correctly, apply Spanish NOM labeling, pay IVA and any duty, and use a licensed customs broker for formal entries.

Do I pay tax on every dropshipped parcel to Mexico?

Usually yes. Mexico's de minimis is only about 117 dollars duty-free for US-origin goods, and a flat 17 percent rate applies between roughly 50 and 117 dollars. So most parcels of real retail value owe tax, which is why importing in bulk and shipping domestically is more profitable than per-parcel imports.

Why is dropshipping to Mexico hard to make profitable?

Because the low de minimis means most parcels owe IVA and possibly duty, and non-US-origin goods face the 2026 tariff decree. Paying those on every individual order erodes thin margins. Bulk importing to a Mexican warehouse and fulfilling domestically spreads the cost and restores margin.

What is the compliant way to dropship into Mexico?

Import inventory in bulk to a warehouse inside Mexico, clear it once through a licensed agente aduanal with correct classification and NOM labeling, then ship each order as a domestic parcel. This keeps every sale compliant while avoiding a customs event on each order.

translations.title: Six Order Checks That Cut Dropshipping Error Rates Into Mexico
translations.excerpt: In domestic dropshipping a bad order costs a reshipment. Across a border it costs a customs delay, a return that is legally an export, and a metric hit. The checks are the same; the stakes are not.
translations.coverAlt: A packing station with an order screen showing a validation prompt beside a sealed parcel held back from the outbound la
translations.metaTitle: Six Order Checks That Cut Dropshipping Errors Into Mexico
translations.metaDescription: A wrong address or a mismatched declaration costs far more across a border than at home. Six checks to run before the order leaves, and what each one prevents.
translations.content:
Run six checks before the order is released: the address resolves, the required address components are present, the description matches the goods, the declared value matches the transaction, the quantity matches, and the destination is one you can serve. Each takes seconds and each prevents a failure that costs days after the goods cross.

  • A wrong address caught before dispatch costs seconds; caught after import it costs a return that is legally an export.
  • Mexican addresses carry a colonia, which is part of the address rather than optional detail, and its absence is a common delivery failure.
  • A description that does not match the goods is a documentation problem that surfaces at the border, not at the warehouse.
  • Most of these checks are automatable, and the ones that are not should stop the order rather than warn about it.

Why does a bad order cost more across a border?

Because the remedies that work domestically are not available once goods have been imported.

Domestic dropshipping has a forgiving failure mode. Wrong address, wrong item, wrong quantity: you apologise, you reship, you absorb the cost, and the customer is usually satisfied. Cross-border, each of those remedies gets harder. A parcel that cannot be delivered in Mexico does not simply come back; returning it is an export from Mexico with its own documentation. A wrong item that has already been imported has been declared as something it is not. A quantity mismatch between the parcel and the paperwork is a discrepancy that gets found at the border rather than at the door. So the same error class carries a much larger cost, and the cost is paid in days rather than in shipping fees. The response is not more care, which does not scale. It is a fixed set of checks that run before every order is released, most of them automatically, and that stop the order rather than flag it. A warning that appears in a queue nobody watches is the same as no check at all.

Which address checks prevent the most failures?

Confirm it resolves to a deliverable location, and confirm the parts a Mexican address needs are present.

Address problems are the single largest source of failed deliveries, and they are the cheapest to prevent. Check one: does the address resolve? Validate against an address service before release, not after a failed delivery. A string that looks plausible and does not resolve is the commonest failure, and it is invisible to a human reading the order. Check two: are the required components present? A Mexican address includes the colonia, the neighborhood-level component that sits between the street and the municipality. It is not optional detail and it is not the same as the district. Storefront forms built for other markets frequently have no field for it, so the customer types it into the street line or omits it entirely, and the parcel arrives at a carrier that cannot route it. Also confirm the postal code is present and consistent with the stated city, since a mismatch there routes a parcel to the wrong region before anyone notices. A practical note on forms. If your checkout has no colonia field for Mexican addresses, no verification step will fix that reliably, because the data was never collected. That is a form change, and it is upstream of everything in this article.

What must the declaration checks confirm?

Description, value and quantity must match what is physically in the box.

These three are one problem viewed from three angles: the paperwork must describe the goods. Check three: does the description match the goods? Generic descriptions carried over from a supplier feed are a recurring source of trouble, because the description on the documentation is what the shipment is assessed against. If the feed says one thing and the box holds another, the mismatch is found at the border. Check four: does the declared value match the transaction? The value stated should reflect what was actually paid. Understating it to reduce charges is not a shortcut, it is a misdeclaration, and the consequences fall on the importer of record rather than on whoever typed the number. Check five: does the quantity match? A supplier shipping a different count than the order is common enough to check every time, and the discrepancy travels: order says three, packing list says three, box holds two, and the problem surfaces at the customer. Where the correct classification or valuation for your product is not obvious, that determination belongs with a specialist for your category rather than with a rule of thumb, and it should be settled once and then applied consistently rather than decided per shipment.

Can you actually serve this destination?

Confirm the destination and the product are both ones your lane supports, before taking the money.

Check six is the one most operations discover they need the hard way. Not every destination inside Mexico is served the same way by every carrier, and not every product can move on every lane. Remote areas carry different timelines. Some product categories have handling requirements that a general parcel lane does not meet. The failure mode is ugly: the order is accepted, the customer is charged and given a date, and then the operation discovers the combination cannot be served on the promised terms. Now you are cancelling an order you already took, which costs more than never having taken it. So maintain a list of what you can serve, by destination type and by product category, and check the order against it before confirming, not after. When something falls outside the list, the honest move is to say so at checkout rather than to accept and hope. This check is also the one that most often reveals a pricing error, because the destinations that are hard to serve are usually the ones your flat shipping rate was not calculated for.

How do you make the checks stick?

Automate what can be automated, block rather than warn, and review what gets blocked.

A checklist that depends on someone remembering is a checklist that works until the first busy week. Automate the mechanical ones. Address resolution, required-component presence, postal code consistency and quantity matching are all rule-based and all automatable. Automate them and let them run on every order without anyone deciding to. Block, do not warn. An order that fails a check should stop and wait for a decision. A warning written to a log is a warning nobody reads. This feels heavy-handed for about a week and then it feels obvious. Review the blocked queue daily, and treat a growing queue as a signal rather than an inconvenience. The pattern in what gets blocked usually points at something upstream: a checkout form missing a field, a supplier feed with bad descriptions, a destination list that needs updating. Measure the error rate before and after. Count orders that failed for a preventable reason as a share of orders shipped, weekly. If the number does not fall after the checks go in, the checks are catching the wrong things and the list needs revisiting rather than enforcing harder.

Required address components presentYesA parcel the local carrier cannot route
Description matches the goodsPartlyA documentation mismatch found at the border
Declared value matches the transactionPartlyA misdeclaration falling on the importer of record
Quantity matches the orderYesA short shipment discovered by the customer
Destination and product are servableYesCancelling an order you already took payment for

Where we catch these

BringGo Ship runs the address and quantity checks on orders that come to us before anything is released, and we stop the ones that fail rather than shipping them and telling you afterwards. When an address arrives without a colonia we ask you for it instead of guessing, because a guess produces a parcel that reaches Mexico and then cannot be routed. We also tell you the count we actually picked against the count on the order, which is where short shipments show up. The checks we cannot run for you are the declaration ones, since only you know what the transaction was.

Definitions

  • Colonia: The neighborhood-level component of a Mexican address, required for routing and frequently missing from checkout forms built for other markets.
  • Importer of record: The party legally responsible for the accuracy of an import declaration and for any charges arising from it.
  • Blocked queue: Orders stopped by a failed check, awaiting a decision, which should be reviewed daily rather than allowed to accumulate.
  • Preventable error rate: Orders that failed for a reason a pre-dispatch check could have caught, as a share of orders shipped.

Frequently asked questions

Which check prevents the most failures?

Address validation, by a wide margin. A large share of cross-border delivery failures are address problems, and they are both the cheapest to catch and the most expensive to fix afterwards, because an undeliverable parcel in Mexico cannot simply be returned the way a domestic one can.

What is a colonia and why does it matter?

It is the neighborhood-level component of a Mexican address, sitting between the street and the municipality. Local carriers route on it. Checkout forms built for other markets often have no field for it, so it never gets collected, and no verification step can recover data that was never captured.

Should a failed check block the order or just warn?

Block it. A warning goes into a log that nobody reads during a busy week, which is exactly when the errors cluster. Blocking feels heavy-handed for about a week and then it feels obvious.

Who is responsible if the declared value is wrong?

The importer of record, not whoever typed the number. That is why understating value is not a cost-saving measure but a liability transfer, and why the correct valuation approach for your product should be settled once with a specialist and then applied consistently.

How do I know the checks are working?

Count orders that failed for a preventable reason as a share of orders shipped, weekly, and measure it before the checks go in as well as after. If it does not fall, the checks are catching the wrong things and the list needs revisiting rather than enforcing harder.

translations.content:
Para etiquetar correctamente en Amazon FBA se aplica el FNSKU, el código de barras propio de Amazon que liga un producto a un vendedor, sobre una etiqueta de entre 1x2 y 2x3 pulgadas, en tinta negra sobre fondo blanco removible, que tape cualquier código de barras original para que solo uno sea escaneable. En 2026 cambió quién debe aplicarlo, aunque esos cambios se anunciaron para Estados Unidos.

  • El FNSKU (Fulfillment Network Stock Keeping Unit) es el código de barras propio de Amazon que liga un producto a un vendedor en FBA (Amazon Seller Central).
  • La etiqueta mide de 1x2 a 2x3 pulgadas, en tinta negra sobre etiqueta blanca removible, y debe tapar cualquier código de barras original para que solo uno sea escaneable (Seller Central).
  • Desde el 1 de enero de 2026, Amazon terminó sus servicios de preparación y etiquetado en FBA de Estados Unidos, así que el vendedor debe etiquetar antes de enviar (Amazon, vía Supply Chain Dive).
  • Para inventario enviado desde el 31 de marzo de 2026, termina el commingling: los revendedores deben aplicar FNSKU incluso con código de fabricante (Seller Forums).
  • Los cambios de 2026 se anunciaron para el FBA de Estados Unidos; conviene verificar su aplicación en México antes de asumirla.

¿Cómo se etiqueta correctamente para FBA?

Se genera el FNSKU en Seller Central y se imprime en una etiqueta de 1x2 a 2x3 pulgadas, en tinta negra sobre fondo blanco removible, que tape cualquier código de barras original para que solo uno sea escaneable. La etiqueta debe mostrar el código escaneable, el FNSKU, el título del producto y su condición.

Etiquetar bien para Amazon FBA es lo que evita que tu inventario se detenga o se confunda en el centro logístico, y todo gira alrededor del FNSKU. El FNSKU, o Fulfillment Network Stock Keeping Unit, es el código de barras propio de Amazon que liga un producto específico a un vendedor específico, y Amazon lo llama simplemente el código de barras de Amazon. Se genera dentro de Seller Central, en Inventario, Administrar inventario, Imprimir etiquetas de producto, y se imprime en láser o térmica a unos 300 DPI. La etiqueta tiene reglas concretas: mide entre 1x2 y 2x3 pulgadas, va en tinta negra sobre una etiqueta blanca, no reflejante y removible, sobre una superficie lisa, evitando esquinas, bordes y curvas. Debe tapar cualquier código de barras original del producto, porque en la caja solo puede haber un código escaneable, y debe mostrar el código escaneable, el FNSKU, el título del producto y su condición. Un detalle práctico: cuando el producto ya trae un código de fabricante escaneable (UPC, EAN), ese suele ser el predeterminado en FBA, y el sticker FNSKU se exige cuando no hay código de fabricante legible, en usados y ciertos productos, o cuando no usas inventario mezclado. Por eso, antes de imprimir, conviene confirmar qué caso aplica a tu producto. BringGo Ship prepara y etiqueta el inventario en su bodega antes de que cruce, de modo que llegue listo tanto para las normas mexicanas como para las reglas de Amazon.

¿Cuándo necesito FNSKU y cuándo basta el código del fabricante?

El código del fabricante (UPC, EAN) es el predeterminado en FBA cuando es legible. El FNSKU se exige cuando no hay código de fabricante escaneable, en usados, medios y ciertos restringidos, o cuando no usas inventario mezclado. Desde el 31 de marzo de 2026, los revendedores deben aplicar FNSKU aunque haya código de fabricante.

Saber cuándo necesitas un FNSKU y cuándo basta el código del fabricante te ahorra trabajo y errores. La regla base es que el código de barras del fabricante, el UPC o EAN, es el predeterminado en FBA siempre que sea escaneable, y en ese caso no necesitarías pegar un FNSKU. El sticker FNSKU se vuelve obligatorio en varios casos: cuando el producto no trae un código de fabricante legible, en artículos usados, medios y ciertos productos restringidos, y cuando no participas en el inventario mezclado, el llamado stickerless commingled. Aquí entra un cambio importante de 2026. Para el inventario enviado a partir del 31 de marzo de 2026, Amazon terminó el commingling con nuevas reglas: los propietarios de marca con el rol de Representante de Marca ya no necesitan sticker FNSKU en productos que traen código de fabricante; en cambio, los revendedores que no son Representantes de Marca deben aplicar FNSKU a todo su inventario FBA, incluso si el producto ya trae código de fabricante; y todos los vendedores siguen necesitando FNSKU en productos sin código de fabricante. En la práctica, esto significa que muchos revendedores que antes dependían del código del fabricante ahora tienen que etiquetar con FNSKU cada unidad. Es una regla que conviene revisar según tu rol en Amazon. BringGo Ship aplica el FNSKU en la preparación, de modo que tu inventario cumple sin importar el caso.

¿Qué cambió en 2026 y aplica en México?

Dos cambios: desde el 1 de enero de 2026 Amazon terminó sus servicios de preparación y etiquetado en el FBA de Estados Unidos, y desde el 31 de marzo de 2026 termina el commingling. Ambos se anunciaron para Estados Unidos, así que su aplicación en México debe verificarse antes de asumirla.

Los cambios de 2026 son importantes, pero hay que leerlos con cuidado sobre a qué mercado aplican, porque ahí está el mayor riesgo de error. El primero: efectivo el 1 de enero de 2026, Amazon terminó sus servicios de preparación y etiquetado en el FBA de Estados Unidos, es decir, dejó de pegar stickers FNSKU, poner bolsas, burbuja o cinta por ti. Ahora el vendedor debe preparar y etiquetar su inventario antes de que llegue al centro logístico, y los envíos creados desde el 1 de enero de 2026 que lleguen sin preparar no son elegibles para reembolso por daño o pérdida. El segundo: para inventario enviado desde el 31 de marzo de 2026 termina el inventario mezclado, con las reglas por rol que ya describimos. El punto clave, y donde muchos se equivocan, es el alcance: ambos cambios se anunciaron a través del Seller Central de Estados Unidos y se refieren al FBA de Estados Unidos. No conviene asumir automáticamente que aplican igual a los centros logísticos de Amazon México; su aplicación en México debe verificarse en la fuente antes de darla por hecha. Lo que sí es global son las mecánicas del FNSKU en sí, que aplican también a México. Por eso la línea segura es: prepara y etiqueta siempre tú, trata las fechas de 2026 como política del FBA de Estados Unidos y confirma su aplicación en México. translations.content:
LTL means less than truckload: your pallets share a trailer with other shippers rather than filling one. Across the US Mexico border, LTL works, but the economics change because customs costs are charged per import declaration rather than per pallet, so consolidating with one importer often beats buying LTL space by the pallet.

  • LTL means your freight shares trailer space instead of filling a dedicated truck.
  • Customs fixed costs are charged per pedimento rather than per pallet, which changes the LTL calculation at the border.
  • Each shipment in a shared trailer may need its own import declaration unless goods are consolidated under one importer.

What is LTL and when does it fit?

LTL is for freight too large for parcel and too small to fill a trailer, typically one to six pallets. You pay for the space you use. Domestically it is straightforward; across the border customs adds a variable that changes the answer.

Less than truckload, or LTL, is the middle option in freight. Below it sits parcel, where you ship boxes individually and pay per package. Above it sits full truckload, where you pay for an entire trailer regardless of how much of it you fill. LTL is what you use when your shipment is bigger than a few boxes but smaller than a truck, typically somewhere between one and six pallets, and the principle is simple: your freight shares a trailer with other shippers and you pay for the space and weight you occupy. Domestically that principle holds cleanly, and LTL pricing follows familiar variables like distance, weight, dimensions and freight class. Across the US Mexico border the transport part still works the same way, but a second cost layer appears that has nothing to do with trucking. Every commercial import into Mexico requires a customs declaration, and the fixed costs attached to that declaration, the broker fee, the prevalidation and the processing charge, are paid per declaration rather than per pallet. So two pallets moving under their own import declaration carry the full weight of those fixed costs, while the same two pallets consolidated into a larger import share them with everything else in that shipment. This is why LTL quotes to Mexico sometimes look reasonable and then land badly: the freight rate was the small number.

Why consolidation usually beats buying LTL by the pallet

Because the customs cost per unit falls when more goods travel under one declaration. Buying LTL space repeatedly means paying the fixed import costs repeatedly. Consolidating at a border warehouse under one importer spreads them.

The practical comparison is not LTL versus full truckload, it is many small imports versus one larger one. Suppose you buy from three suppliers and each sends two pallets. If each moves separately across the border, you are looking at separate declarations and the fixed customs costs are incurred each time. If instead all three deliver to a warehouse on the US side, the goods are received, checked, consolidated and cross the border as a single import, those fixed costs are paid once and spread across six pallets. The freight portion may be similar either way; the customs portion is not close. There is a second saving that people underestimate. Consolidation gives you a place to prepare goods before they cross, which for Mexico means Spanish NOM labelling. Applying labels at a border warehouse while cartons are open and staffed costs a fraction of relabelling per unit after arrival, and it removes the most common reason goods are held at the border. And there is a third, less obvious benefit: fewer border events means fewer opportunities for something to go wrong. Every import declaration is a chance for a classification error, a document mismatch or a red light inspection. Reducing the number of crossings reduces the number of times you roll those dice. None of this makes LTL wrong. It makes buying LTL repeatedly without consolidating an expensive default.

When LTL is still the right call

When you have one shipment from one supplier going to one destination and no reason to wait for other goods. Also when timing matters more than cost, because consolidation means waiting for the next crossing.

Consolidation is not always the answer and it is worth being honest about when it is not. If you have a single shipment from a single supplier, there is nothing to consolidate with; you are simply moving freight and LTL is exactly the right tool. If your goods are urgent and the next consolidated crossing is several days away, waiting to save on fixed costs can be the wrong trade, because a stockout usually costs more than a broker fee. If your volume is already large enough to fill a trailer to one destination, you have moved past both options and full truckload will be cheaper per unit. And if your buyer in Mexico is the importer of record and handles their own clearance, the customs arithmetic sits on their side rather than yours, which changes the picture entirely. The rule that covers most situations is this: if you import from more than one source, or more than once a month, consolidation is almost certainly cheaper than buying LTL by the pallet, and the difference grows with frequency. If you import rarely, from one place, to one place, LTL on its own is fine. Whichever route you choose, transit is not the deciding factor. A well documented truck reaches Monterrey from Laredo in one to two business days, and documentation quality affects that timeline far more than the freight mode does.   • LTL: LTL, or less than truckload, means your pallets share a trailer with other shippers and you pay for the space you use.

LTL means less than truckload: your pallets share a trailer with other shippers rather than filling one, and you pay for the space and weight you occupy. It fits freight too large for parcel and too small for a full truck, typically one to six pallets. Across the border, customs costs change the calculation.

Why is LTL to Mexico more expensive than it looks?

Because the freight rate is only part of it. Every commercial import needs a customs declaration, and the fixed costs attached, the broker fee, prevalidation and processing charge, are paid per declaration rather than per pallet. Moving small shipments separately means paying those fixed costs every time.

Is consolidation always cheaper than LTL?

Not always. If you have one shipment from one supplier to one destination, there is nothing to consolidate with and LTL is the right tool. If goods are urgent and the next consolidated crossing is days away, waiting can cost more than it saves. Consolidation wins when you buy from several sources or ship regularly.

A place to prepare goods before they cross. Spanish NOM labelling can be applied at the border warehouse while cartons are open, which costs far less than relabelling per unit in Mexico and removes the most common reason goods are held. It also means fewer border events and fewer chances of an error.

How long does LTL take from the US to Mexico?

A well documented truck reaches Monterrey from Laredo in one to two business days, because the distance is a few hours of driving plus clearance. Documentation quality affects that timeline far more than the freight mode does, so a clean file matters more than whether the goods travelled LTL or consolidated.

translations.metaDescription: The RFC is Mexico's tax ID. It controls whether you can import, how much marketplaces withhold, and whether you can invoice. Who actually needs one.
keywords: do I need an RFC in Mexico
translations.content:
The RFC (Registro Federal de Contribuyentes) is Mexico's tax identification number, issued by SAT to individuals and companies with Mexican tax obligations. You need one to enrol in the padrón de importadores and import commercially, to issue CFDI electronic invoices, and to avoid maximum marketplace withholding. A foreign company cannot obtain an RFC without establishing Mexican tax presence, which is why foreign sellers typically work through a structure that holds one.

  • The RFC is issued by SAT and is required for enrolment in the padrón de importadores, without which commercial importing is not possible.
  • Issuing a CFDI, Mexico's mandatory electronic invoice, requires an RFC and an active e.firma.
  • Marketplaces withhold at maximum rates from sellers who have not provided a valid RFC: 20 percent ISR and the full 16 percent IVA.
  • An RFC brings ongoing obligations, including periodic returns that must be filed whether or not there was activity in the period.
  • Enrolment in the padrón de importadores additionally requires a positive opinión de cumplimiento, so outstanding tax issues block the application.

What is the RFC and what does it unlock?

It is Mexico's tax ID, and it is the prerequisite for importing, invoicing, and being treated as an ordinary taxpayer rather than an unidentified one.

The RFC is the identifier SAT uses for every taxpayer in Mexico. Structurally it is similar to a tax identification number elsewhere, but its practical reach in commercial operations is wider than most foreign sellers expect. Three things depend on it. Importing: enrolment in the padrón de importadores requires an RFC, and without padrón enrolment you cannot be the importer of record on a commercial shipment. Invoicing: Mexican business customers require a CFDI, the electronic invoice, to deduct their purchase, and issuing one requires an RFC and a valid e.firma. Withholding: marketplaces apply maximum rates to sellers without an RFC. There is a fourth, less obvious effect. Mexican B2B buyers frequently will not transact with a supplier who cannot issue a CFDI, because the purchase becomes non-deductible for them. This is not a preference; it is an accounting consequence. If your Mexico plan involves selling to businesses, the RFC is not optional in any practical sense.

Can a foreign company get an RFC?

Not without Mexican tax presence. In practice this means a Mexican legal entity, a permanent establishment, or working through a structure that already holds one.

An RFC is issued to taxpayers with Mexican tax obligations. A company incorporated in the United States, Turkey or Spain with no Mexican presence does not have those obligations and cannot simply apply. The routes that do work are three. Incorporating a Mexican entity, typically an S. de R.L. or S.A. de C.V., which then obtains its own RFC. Registering a permanent establishment, which is appropriate in narrower circumstances and carries its own tax consequences. Or contracting with a Mexican entity that acts as importer of record and, where relevant, as the invoicing party. The third is what most cross-border e-commerce sellers use, and it is what Amazon expects when it asks a foreign seller for a FIOR. It is legitimate. It is also a genuine allocation of legal responsibility: the Mexican entity is answerable to SAT and to customs for what is declared under its registration, which is why these arrangements are contractual rather than casual. The wrong approach is to borrow someone's RFC informally. The registration carries liability, and using another party's registration without a proper arrangement exposes both sides.

What does having an RFC oblige you to do?

File periodic returns, maintain a positive compliance opinion, keep the fiscal address current, and hold a valid e.firma.

An RFC is not a one-time registration you obtain and forget. It creates recurring obligations, and the cost of neglecting them shows up at the worst moment. Periodic returns must be filed even for periods with no activity. A dormant entity that stops filing accumulates omissions, and those omissions turn the opinión de cumplimiento negative. That compliance opinion matters more than it sounds. It is required for padrón de importadores enrolment and is checked for various procedures. An importer who lets it lapse can find shipments blocked not because of anything wrong with the shipment, but because a return was missed months earlier. The e.firma, Mexico's advanced electronic signature, must be kept valid. It expires, and renewal requires an appointment. Companies discover this when they need to file something urgently and cannot. The fiscal address must be real and locatable. SAT verifies addresses, and a domicile that cannot be verified can move the taxpayer status to non-localised, which cascades into the compliance opinion. None of this is onerous with a competent Mexican accountant. All of it is expensive to fix retroactively.

Definitions

  • e.firma: The e.firma is Mexico's advanced electronic signature, required for filing returns, issuing invoices and completing SAT procedures, and it expires and must be renewed.
  • Opinión de cumplimiento: The opinión de cumplimiento is SAT's compliance status certificate, which must be positive for padrón enrolment and various other procedures.
  • CFDI: A CFDI is Mexico's mandatory electronic invoice, which Mexican business buyers require in order to deduct a purchase.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need an RFC to sell on Amazon Mexico?

You can sell without one, but Amazon will withhold at maximum rates: 20 percent ISR and the full 16 percent IVA. Without Mexican tax registration the withheld IVA is generally not recoverable.

Can a US or Turkish company obtain a Mexican RFC?

Not directly. An RFC requires Mexican tax obligations, which means a Mexican entity or permanent establishment. Foreign sellers commonly work through a Mexican entity acting as importer of record instead.

Do I need an RFC to import into Mexico?

Yes. Enrolment in the padrón de importadores requires an RFC, and commercial imports require padrón enrolment. The importer of record must therefore be a Mexican registered taxpayer.

What happens if I have an RFC but stop filing?

Omitted returns turn your opinión de cumplimiento negative, which can block padrón enrolment and other procedures. Returns must be filed even for periods with no activity.

Nuevo León, con Monterrey como centro, concentra buena parte de la ola de nearshoring en México por tres razones: su cercanía a la frontera de Laredo, el puerto terrestre más transitado de Norteamérica; su base industrial y de talento consolidada; y su red de parques industriales y logística. Que tu producción o tu almacén quedan a 1 o 2 días de la frontera. Un almacén en Monterrey te da distribución nacional dentro de México y, a la vez, un acceso rápido a Laredo para cruzar hacia Estados Unidos o recibir mercancía de allá, todo en un tránsito de 1 a 2 días hábiles.

translations.content:
La NOM-004 exige que los textiles y la ropa importados a México lleven, en español, cinco datos clave: la composición de fibras por porcentaje en orden descendente, las instrucciones de cuidado, la talla o dimensiones, el nombre y RFC del responsable en México, y el país de origen. En prendas, la etiqueta principal debe ser permanente y estar cosida. Sin esta etiqueta, la mercancía se detiene en la aduana.

  • La NOM-004-SCFI rige la información comercial de textiles, ropa y textiles del hogar importados y vendidos en México (DOF).
  • Exige, en español: composición de fibras por nombre genérico y porcentaje en peso, en orden descendente.
  • Exige instrucciones de cuidado, talla o dimensiones, y el nombre y RFC del responsable (fabricante o importador) en México.
  • Exige el país de origen con la leyenda Hecho en, y en prendas la etiqueta principal debe ser permanente y cosida.
  • Sin etiqueta NOM-004 correcta, la mercancía textil se detiene en la aduana; prepararla antes de cruzar lo evita.

¿Qué etiqueta exige la NOM-004 en textiles?

Cinco datos en español: composición de fibras por porcentaje en orden descendente, instrucciones de cuidado, talla o dimensiones, nombre y RFC del responsable en México, y país de origen. En prendas, la etiqueta principal debe ser permanente y cosida. Es la información comercial mínima para importar y vender textiles.

La NOM-004 es la norma que define qué debe decir la etiqueta de los textiles, la ropa y los textiles del hogar que se importan y venden en México, y cumplirla es lo que separa una importación que fluye de una que se detiene. Exige cinco datos, todos en español. El primero es la composición de fibras: hay que declarar cada fibra por su nombre genérico y su porcentaje en peso, ordenados de mayor a menor, por ejemplo algodón 60 por ciento, poliéster 40 por ciento. El segundo son las instrucciones de cuidado: cómo lavar, secar y planchar la prenda, normalmente con símbolos y texto. El tercero es la talla o las dimensiones, según sea ropa o textil del hogar como sábanas o toallas. El cuarto es el responsable: el nombre y el RFC del fabricante o del importador en México, es decir, quién responde por el producto dentro del país. El quinto es el país de origen, con la leyenda Hecho en seguida del país. Además del contenido, importa la forma: en prendas de vestir, la etiqueta principal con esta información debe ser permanente y estar cosida, no ser un colgante que se quita. Reunir estos cinco datos en español, colocados correctamente, es lo que exige la NOM-004, y hacerlo antes de que la mercancía cruce evita que se detenga en la aduana. BringGo Ship prepara el etiquetado NOM en español y el expediente de los textiles, para que el agente aduanal que presenta tu pedimento los ingrese en regla.

¿Por qué se detienen los textiles en la aduana?

Casi siempre por la etiqueta: falta un dato de la NOM-004, está en inglés en lugar de español, o la etiqueta no es permanente en prendas. También por una clasificación arancelaria incorrecta. La mercancía textil se detiene cuando la etiqueta no cumple, no por el producto en sí.

Entender por qué se detienen los textiles es la forma más rápida de evitarlo, porque las causas se repiten y son prevenibles. La más común es la etiqueta: la NOM-004 pide cinco datos específicos en español, y basta que falte uno, que la composición o el cuidado estén en inglés, o que la etiqueta en una prenda no sea permanente y cosida, para que la mercancía se retenga. La segunda causa es la colocación y permanencia: en ropa, una etiqueta colgante o removible no cumple con el requisito de etiqueta principal permanente, aunque el contenido sea correcto. La tercera es la clasificación arancelaria: un textil mal clasificado puede detenerse mientras la aduana lo resuelve. Nota lo que casi nunca es el problema: el producto en sí, porque un textil bien fabricado se detiene igual si su etiqueta no cumple. La lección práctica es que el etiquetado no es un detalle final sino el requisito que decide si la mercancía pasa, y que revisarlo contra la NOM-004 antes de cruzar, cuando corregirlo es barato, evita el costo y la demora de una retención en la frontera. Esto es exactamente el trabajo que conviene hacer en un almacén de frontera, con la mercancía y las etiquetas en el mismo lugar, en lugar de descubrir el problema en la aduana. BringGo Ship revisa y coloca el etiquetado NOM-004 en español antes de que los textiles crucen, lo que es lo que evita que se detengan.

¿Cómo preparas tus textiles para cumplir la NOM-004?

Reúne los cinco datos en español, coloca la etiqueta principal permanente y cosida en prendas, verifica la clasificación arancelaria, y hazlo antes de que la mercancía cruce, en un almacén de frontera. Un operador con etiquetado NOM y agente aduanal deja los textiles listos para entrar en regla.

Preparar los textiles para cumplir la NOM-004 es una secuencia clara, y seguirla en orden es lo que mantiene la mercancía en movimiento. Primero, reúne los cinco datos en español: la composición de fibras por porcentaje en orden descendente, las instrucciones de cuidado, la talla o dimensiones, el nombre y RFC del responsable en México, y el país de origen con la leyenda Hecho en. Segundo, cuida la forma: en prendas, la etiqueta principal con esta información debe ser permanente y cosida, así que planifica el etiquetado desde la producción o en la preparación previa al cruce, no como un pegado de último momento. Tercero, verifica la clasificación arancelaria del textil con tu agente aduanal, porque una clasificación incorrecta detiene igual que una etiqueta incompleta. Cuarto, y este es el punto que ahorra más, haz todo esto antes de que la mercancía cruce, idealmente en un almacén de frontera donde la mercancía y las etiquetas están juntas, en lugar de descubrir un problema en la aduana. Cinco datos en español: composición de fibras por porcentaje en orden descendente, instrucciones de cuidado, talla o dimensiones, nombre y RFC del responsable en México, y país de origen con la leyenda Hecho en. En prendas, la etiqueta principal debe ser permanente y cosida. Es la información comercial mínima para importar y vender textiles.

¿La etiqueta debe estar en español?

Sí. La NOM-004 exige que la información, la composición, el cuidado, la talla, el responsable y el país de origen, esté en español. Una etiqueta en inglés, aunque tenga todos los datos, no cumple y es una de las causas más comunes de que la mercancía textil se detenga en la aduana.
