Mal ABD'de satılmayacaksa mevzuat iki araç sunuyor. Bonded depoda ithalat vergisi mal çıkana kadar ertelenir. Serbest bölgede mal henüz ABD'ye ithal edilmiş sayılmaz, dolayısıyla oradan Meksika'ya çıkan malda ABD vergisi hiç doğmayabilir. Hangisinin uygun olduğunu gümrük müşavirinle netleştir.

Laredo'da ne yapılıyor?

Teslim alma ve sayım, konsolidasyon, İspanyolca NOM etiketleme ve belge hazırlığı. Konsolidasyon en değerli kısmı: Meksika tarafındaki sabit maliyetler pedimento başına ödendiği için, birden fazla sevkiyatı tek ithalatta birleştirmek birim maliyeti belirgin şekilde düşürüyor.

translations.title: US Return Address For Mexican Sellers: Handling Northbound Returns
translations.excerpt: A Mexican seller reaching US customers hits the same wall in reverse: without a US return address, every return becomes an export and the cost usually exceeds the product.
translations.coverAlt: Returned packages being logged at a warehouse receiving desk, photographic, no text
translations.metaTitle: US Return Address for Mexican Sellers: Northbound Returns
translations.metaDescription: Selling to US customers from Mexico means US buyers expect a US return address. What happens without one, and how to process northbound returns cheaply.
keywords: US return address for Mexican sellers
translations.content:
A Mexican seller selling to US customers needs a return address inside the United States. Without one, each return is an international shipment whose cost usually exceeds the value of the product. With one, the return is a domestic parcel, the unit can be inspected and restocked in the US, and only the small share worth recovering travels south consolidated.

  • US buyers expect a domestic return address and compare your policy against local sellers.
  • Without a US address, each return becomes an international shipment with its own formalities and cost.
  • Returned units in resellable condition can go straight back into US sellable stock rather than crossing the border twice.
  • Only the minority of units genuinely worth recovering should travel south, and they should travel consolidated.
  • A well documented truck covers Monterrey to Laredo in one to two business days (operational data).

How do Mexican sellers handle returns from US customers?

By having an address inside the United States that receives them. It does not need to be your own facility. What matters is that the buyer ships domestically and that someone inspects the unit before deciding what happens to it.

A Mexican company selling into the United States runs into the mirror image of the problem US sellers face going south, and it is worth stating plainly because the solution is the same shape. Your US customer expects to return the way they return to any local store: print a label, drop the parcel, get refunded. If your only return address is in Mexico, that is not what happens. The parcel becomes an international shipment, it needs documentation, it moves at international speed, and the cost of moving one item is wildly out of proportion to the item itself. In most consumer categories the return shipping alone exceeds the product value, which pushes sellers into two bad habits: refusing returns, which damages the listing and invites disputes, or refunding without recovering the goods, which means eating the full cost of every return. The third option is an address inside the United States. It does not have to be a facility you own; a logistics partner operating there provides the same thing. The customer ships domestically, which is fast and cheap for them, the parcel arrives in days rather than weeks, and you get the thing that actually matters: possession of the unit and the ability to inspect it before deciding what it is worth. That single change turns returns from a fixed loss into a recovery process.

What to do with the unit once it arrives

Log it against the order, grade it, then send it down one of three paths: back into US sellable stock, into a secondary channel, or disposal. Sending it back to Mexico should be the exception, and when it happens it should be consolidated.

A return address is just a mailbox until there is a process behind it, and the process is short. Step one is intake: record what arrived and match it to an order, because an unmatched return is a refund dispute waiting to happen. Step two is inspection and grading, sorting units honestly into condition tiers rather than treating them as one pile. From there, three paths. Units in resellable condition go straight back into your US inventory and sell again to the next US customer. This is the path that makes the whole model pay, because the unit becomes revenue without crossing any border in either direction. Units with damaged packaging or light wear go to a secondary channel, which depending on your category might be a discounted listing, a refurbished offer or a bundle. Units that are genuinely unsellable go to disposal, and it is worth being decisive here rather than paying to store things that will never sell. Only after this sorting does sending anything to Mexico make sense. Usually the answer is that a minority of units justify it, and when they do they should travel together in one consolidated shipment rather than one at a time. A well documented truck covers Monterrey to Laredo in one to two business days, so batching costs you very little time and saves a great deal of money.

Setting it up, and the second thing it buys you

Decide who receives, publish a clear English return policy, write down grading rules, and set a consolidation rhythm. The same US facility that handles returns also serves as the forward stocking point that makes your US delivery times competitive.

Four decisions get this running. First, who receives the returns. Very few Mexican sellers need their own US facility for this, because returns volume is a fraction of outbound volume and a lease plus staff rarely pays for itself; most use a partner already operating there. Second, what the customer sees: a return policy in English, easy to find, specific about the window, the condition expected and how the refund is issued. Vague policies generate support tickets and chargebacks rather than clean returns. Third, the grading rulebook, written before the first return arrives so the decision does not depend on who opens the box. Fourth, the consolidation rhythm, meaning how often the small number of recoverable units travel south. Then there is a second benefit that often matters more than the returns themselves. The same US facility that receives returns can hold forward stock for US orders. Once you have inventory sitting in the United States, your US delivery times stop being international and start being domestic, which is the single biggest factor in whether a US buyer chooses you over a local seller. In other words, the infrastructure you build to stop losing money on returns is the same infrastructure that lets you compete properly in that market. BringGo Ship runs warehouses in Laredo and Monterrey, so a US return point, inspection, restocking and consolidated southbound shipments sit in one chain.

Definitions

  • Northbound return: A northbound return is a product sent back by a US customer to a seller based in Mexico.
  • Grading: Grading is sorting returned units by condition so each follows the right path: restock, secondary channel or disposal.
  • Forward stock: Forward stock is inventory held inside the destination market so orders ship domestically rather than internationally.

Frequently asked questions

Do Mexican sellers need a US return address?

In practice yes, if you sell to US consumers. Buyers expect to return the way they do to any local store. Without a US address each return is an international shipment whose cost usually exceeds the product value, which pushes sellers into refusing returns or refunding without recovering the goods.

Does the return address have to be my own facility?

No. Returns volume is normally a fraction of outbound volume, so a lease and staff rarely pay for themselves. Most Mexican sellers use a logistics partner already operating in the United States. What matters is that the buyer ships domestically and that someone inspects the unit before deciding what it is worth.

What happens to returned units that are still good?

They go straight back into your US sellable stock and sell again to the next US customer. This is the path that makes the model pay, because the unit becomes revenue without crossing any border in either direction. Sending it home to Mexico would mean paying to move it twice for no gain.

Should I ship returns back to Mexico?

Only the minority where recovered value clearly justifies it, and then consolidated rather than one at a time. A well documented truck covers Monterrey to Laredo in one to two business days, so batching costs very little time and saves a great deal of money compared with individual shipments.

Is there any benefit beyond cheaper returns?

Yes, and it is often bigger. The same US facility can hold forward stock for US orders. Once inventory sits in the United States your delivery times stop being international and become domestic, which is the main factor in whether a US buyer chooses you over a local seller.

translations.title: USPS To Mexico: Where The Tracking Stops And What Sellers Use Instead
translations.excerpt: USPS does not deliver in Mexico. It carries your parcel to a handover point and passes it to the Mexican postal operator, and most of what sellers experience as a tracking failure is actually that handover working exactly as designed.
translations.coverAlt: A parcel sorting facility with a clear division between two handling zones and a conveyor crossing between them, wide an
translations.metaTitle: USPS To Mexico: Where Tracking Stops And What To Use
translations.metaDescription: USPS hands your parcel to the Mexican postal service at the border. Here is what that means for tracking, for delivery expectations and for your seller metrics.
translations.content:
USPS carries your parcel to the handover with the Mexican postal operator and no further. After that, scanning depends on what the receiving service transmits back, which is why tracking appears to stop at the border. For marketplace orders judged on delivery dates, sellers generally use a carrier whose scan record continues to the door.

  • USPS states that Priority Mail Express International and Priority Mail International include international tracking, which is not the same as tracking that continues to the door in every destination.
  • The handover to the destination postal operator is the point at which USPS visibility depends on what the receiving service transmits back.
  • A tracking number that stops updating looks identical to one that never worked, and both can affect a seller's valid tracking rate.
  • Delivery in Mexico under a postal service is performed by the Mexican postal operator, not by USPS.

What does USPS actually sell you on a Mexico route?

Carriage to a handover point, plus whatever visibility the receiving postal service chooses to return.

Sellers often read an international postal service as an end-to-end delivery product. It is not, and understanding the structure explains almost every complaint that follows. A postal item bound for Mexico travels under USPS custody to a handover point. There it passes to the destination country's postal operator, which performs the final delivery. This is the standard structure of international postal exchange and it applies broadly, not only to Mexico. USPS is explicit about which of its services carry tracking. On its international shipping page it states that "Priority Mail Express International® and Priority Mail International® services include international tracking and some insurance." That statement is accurate and it is also narrower than it first appears. Tracking is included, but after the handover the scan events are generated by the receiving operator, and what USPS can display is limited to what that operator transmits back. Where a destination service returns little data, the tracking record thins out or stops, even though the parcel is moving normally.

Why does the tracking appear to die at the border?

Because visibility changes hands at the same moment the parcel does.

The experience is consistent enough that sellers treat it as a defect. A parcel scans reliably across the United States, reaches the border area, and then produces nothing for days. In most cases nothing has gone wrong. The parcel has been handed over, and the new custodian's scan data is either not shared back or shared on a delay. The USPS record has no more to show because USPS no longer has the parcel. The practical workaround is to check the destination operator's own tracking with the same number, since the item generally retains its identifier through the handover. That will often reveal events the origin carrier never displayed. But a workaround for you is not a solution for your customer, who is looking at the tracking link in their order confirmation and drawing the obvious conclusion. And it is not a solution for the marketplace either, which is reading the same silence you are.

What does the tracking silence do to a seller metric?

A parcel that arrives on time but stops scanning can still be recorded as a shipment without valid tracking.

This is where a postal route stops being merely inconvenient and starts being expensive. Marketplaces assess whether a shipment carried a tracking number that produced real carrier events. A number that goes quiet after the handover may fail that assessment even if the parcel is delivered perfectly and on schedule. From the marketplace's position, an unverifiable delivery and a failed one look similar. The second effect is on the customer, and it arrives sooner. A buyer watching a tracking page that has not moved for several days will contact you, and a proportion of those contacts become claims regardless of the eventual outcome. Those claims reach your order defect rate. So the calculation for a marketplace seller is not simply postage cost against carrier cost. It is postage cost against carrier cost plus the value of a scan record that continues to the door, and on a marketplace where metrics gate your visibility, that record is worth considerably more than the difference in postage.

When is a postal service still the right choice?

Low value, no promised date, tolerant recipient, and no marketplace metric attached.

None of this makes postal services wrong. It makes them wrong for a specific use, and right for others. A postal route remains reasonable when the parcel is low in value, when nobody has been given a firm delivery date, when the recipient is a person who will wait, and above all when there is no marketplace scorecard reading the tracking. Sample shipments, replacement parts to a patient customer, personal items and low-stakes direct sales all fit. It becomes the wrong choice as soon as a delivery promise has been made and something is measuring whether you kept it. That is the line, and it is not about parcel size or distance. The alternatives for that second case are a commercial express carrier, which maintains its own network and scan record into Mexico, or a consolidated cross-border service, where volume moves under one controlled movement and is injected for domestic delivery inside Mexico with a domestic tracking record. Which of those is cheaper depends entirely on your volume, and it is a question worth actually calculating rather than assuming.

What should you check before committing to a lane?

Ask where custody changes, what the customer sees at that moment, and what the record looks like afterwards.

Whatever route you choose, three questions separate a service that will hold up from one that will generate support tickets. First, where does custody change hands. Every cross-border option has at least one handover, and knowing where it is tells you where visibility is at risk. Second, what does the customer's tracking page show at that moment. Some services present a continuous record across the handover. Others present a gap, and a gap is what generates the message asking where the parcel is. Third, what does the record look like after the handover, and can you retrieve it without asking the customer to check a second website. If the answer requires your buyer to visit another tracking page in another language, the route will cost you in support time even when it delivers on schedule. Ask those three questions of any provider, including a postal service, and the right lane for your particular mix of value, urgency and metric exposure usually becomes obvious.

Choosing a lane into Mexico by what is at stake

SituationUsual fitWhy
Low value, no promised date, no marketplacePostal serviceCost dominates and tracking gaps are tolerable
Marketplace order with a delivery promiseCommercial carrierScan record continues and supports the metric
Regular volume on a fixed routeConsolidated cross-border serviceOne controlled movement, domestic delivery record
Urgent, high value, single parcelCommercial expressSpeed and custody outweigh unit cost

How we keep the record continuous

BringGo Ship moves seller volume from our Laredo warehouse into Mexico as a controlled movement and injects it for delivery inside the country, which means the record your customer sees does not depend on what a foreign postal operator chooses to transmit back. When custody changes on our lane, we tell you where and when it changed rather than leaving a silent gap in the tracking page. If you are currently sending marketplace orders by post and getting messages asking where the parcel is, that silence is usually the reason, and it is the part we can remove.

Definitions

  • Handover: The point at which one carrier passes custody of a parcel to another, which on a postal route is where origin-carrier visibility ends.
  • Destination postal operator: The national postal service that performs final delivery in the receiving country, which in Mexico is the Mexican postal service rather than USPS.
  • Valid tracking rate: A marketplace measure of the share of shipments whose tracking number produced real, verifiable carrier scan events.
  • Consolidated cross-border service: A model where many parcels move together under one controlled border movement and are then injected for domestic delivery in the destination country.

Frequently asked questions

Does USPS deliver parcels in Mexico?

No. USPS carries the item to a handover point and the destination postal operator performs delivery inside Mexico. This is the standard structure of international postal exchange, and it is why tracking visibility changes at that point.

Why did my USPS tracking stop updating?

Usually because the parcel was handed over and the receiving operator's scan data is not shared back, or is shared on a delay. The parcel is generally moving normally. Checking the same number on the destination operator's own tracking often shows events USPS never displayed.

Do USPS international services include tracking?

USPS states that Priority Mail Express International and Priority Mail International include international tracking and some insurance. That is accurate, but after the handover the events shown depend on what the receiving postal service transmits back.

Can a tracking gap affect my seller metrics?

Yes. A number that stops producing verifiable events can fail a valid tracking assessment even when the parcel arrives on time, and the customer messages generated by a silent tracking page can turn into claims that reach your order defect rate.

When is a postal service still the right choice into Mexico?

When the value is low, no firm delivery date has been promised, the recipient will wait, and no marketplace scorecard is reading the tracking. As soon as a delivery promise is being measured, the scan record is usually worth more than the postage saving.
